items.title: I Tried Deepseek's New SuperAgent Harness... Is IT ANY GOOD?
items.summary:
Join this channel to get access to perks:

DeepSeek Harness article (Exploring Super-agent Design): https://x.com/DeepSeekHarness/status/2116857257245987236
dsh-superagent prototype (research code): https://github.com/deepseek-ai/dsh-superagent-prototype
PandaCode: https://github.com/aicodeking/pandacode
Cline Desktop: https://docs.cline.bot/usage/cline-desktop
ClinePass: https://docs.cline.bot/getting-started/clinepass

In this video, I'll go through DeepSeek Harness's article "Exploring Super-agent Design", which starts from a simple problem: agents can now work on their own, but you can only follow about 3 to 5 sessions at once. I'll explain the design: the four things a Super-agent needs, the Router and Workers split, Triggers with two filters, Chain of Recall, the Watchdog, and what their experiment on synthetic workloads actually shows. Then I'll show how I would build a practical version today with PandaCode bots, using a cheap De
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: Hi, welcome to another video. So, the Deep Seek Harness team just published a long article called Exploring Super Agent Design and I think it is one of the most useful things I have read about coding agents this year because it isn't selling a model or a feature. It starts from a problem that you have probably felt already. The agents got good enough to work on their own and now the thing slowing you down is you. They say that a person can usually follow only three to five active sessions at once, and that sounds right to me. Past that point, you forget which session knows what. One of them has been waiting on an approval for 20 minutes, and two of them are touching the same pull request. A single task is limited by the model, but running many tasks is limited by your attention. So, their idea is to stop making the session the thing you manage. You talk to one agent in the places where you already work, like your team chat and your GitHub comments, and the system creates and manages the sessions behind it. They call this a super agent. Now, one important thing before we start. This article is about architecture. It is not a list of features that Deep Seek Caress has today. They also published a prototype on GitHub called DSH Super Agent. And they say clearly that it is research code and not an official product. So, you can't just install the system from the article, but you can use a lot of these ideas right now. So, in this video, I want to explain how the design works and then show you how I would build a version of it in Pandaode with client pass for the models and client desktop for the recurring jobs. So, let's get right into it. >> The article says that a super agent needs four things. It has to be continuous, which means it always feels like one agent. So, you can ask for plan A in the chat, switch to plan B in a pull request comment, and it understands the change. It has to be productive, so it can take your next instruction before the last task is finished. It has to be proactive, so it watches what is happening and acts on what matters without being told. and it has to be persistent so it stays online and recovers when something breaks. The first big idea is the one I like the most and it comes from a simple trade-off. If you send every event to one session, you get perfect context, but that session can only do one thing at a time and the details of different tasks get mixed together. If you give every event its own new session, you get a lot of speed, but nothing is connected and you get several agents all replying to you separately. So, they split it into two layers. The first layer is the router, which is one longived session that talks to people and hands out work. It doesn't do the work itself, and it can even run without a bash tool. The second layer is the workers. Each worker gets one task and its own clean context, and it never talks to people directly. It only reports back to the router, so you only ever hear from one agent. This also flips how you would normally pick your models. The router's job is simpler than it looks, so a lighter model is usually enough. The workers are the ones writing the code, so that is where your best model should go. And it is different from a normal agent team where the lead has to deeply understand the task and split it into steps. This router doesn't split anything. It just decides who gets what and keeps track of how the tasks relate. The second big idea is that prompts stop being the main input. Group chat messages, emails, review comments, and CI results all become events and they call those events triggers. Most of them are noise and you don't want a big model reading everyone. So they use two filters. Normal code removes what it can first using things like the source of the event and allow lists. Only what survives goes to the model which decides based on rules that you write in plain language. There is a clever part here too. Once a worker owns a task, it subscribes to that task's thread like a pull request. And new events on that thread go straight to the worker. The router still sees them, but it doesn't have to forward them. And if two workers are on the same pull request, they both get the same events, so they can notice a conflict on their own. They also treat the context window like a cache. The model first gets an ID and a short summary, then the things it will probably need next, and anything long gets cut off with a pointer to the rest. Since every object links to related objects by ID, the router can follow those links back to an old task when you bring it up weeks later. They call that chain of recall. And then there is the part that feels a little like the future. In their own user group, they set a policy called silently reproduce and fix. When someone reports an issue, the agent tries to reproduce it in the background, and if it confirms the issue and finds a simple fix. It opens a pull request while people are still discussing it. If it doesn't, you never hear about it. That is pretty amazing, to be honest. The rest of the design is about keeping this alive. Long commands run in the background, so the agent can still answer you while they run. Replies change by channel, and they found that a hard limit of 100 words per chat reply works well with the detailed writing kept for pull requests. The agent loop and the saved state live in the cloud while your real machine stays where it is and runs a small Damon that just executes commands and a separate watchdog session runs on a schedule because a stuck agent usually isn't a crashed process. The process looks healthy but the model is going in circles or has drifted from the goal. Now the experiment is really interesting but take it with a grain of salt because they say themselves that the results are only indicative. They used about 300 messages per run. About 20 of them were real work requests and the coding was simulated by a tool that just uses up time. So this tests the scheduling and not the quality of the code. The super agent finished a typical task in 12.4 minutes and 15.7 at the slow end. A single session with a neutral prompt that said to use a sub agent when appropriate, didn't call a sub aent in any of its five runs, and its slow end reached 29.5 minutes. with a prompt that pushed hard for delegation. It delegated in four of five runs. And in the fifth, it decided the work was small and did it all itself. If you ask me, that is the most useful result in the whole article. You can't rely on a prompt to make a model delegate. You have to make it the structure of the system. The router also held up better than you would expect. As they went from about 1 to about 40 decisions per minute, events started to batch together, and the time per decision dropped from 6.4 seconds to 1.6. So one router session is enough for a team of their size and there is no need to split it early. There is a cost though. Several sessions read a lot more cached tokens. A super agent run used 23.2 million cash read tokens and even that needed their pass through system because without it the number went up to 31.8 million. Now this is where a cheap model changes the maths. At DeepSeek V4.1 flash off peak pricing 23.2 2 million cached tokens cost about 7. At sonnet 5.5 pricing, the same cash tokens cost about $4.64. That is only the cash reads from one synthetic run. But you can see why this design makes much more sense on cheap models. And they are honest about what is not solved. Long-term memory is still the main limit. Once a system has been running for months, and security is a big one. An agent that reads outside events is exposed to prompt injection. So if the cloud loop gets compromised, every machine connected to it could be taken over. Please keep that in mind before you connect this to a public group chat. So, how do you use these ideas today? This is how I would do it in Pandode. If you don't know it, Pandode is my free and open source desktop app that runs all your coding agents in one window, including DeepSeek through its own harness and Klein. It isn't a super agent, and I will show you exactly where it falls short. But the pieces for a practical version are already there, mostly in a feature called bots. A bot is a persistent agent that you can message from Telegram, Slack, Discord, WhatsApp, or a local web chat. It has its own memory, schedules, and rules. And every conversation is a normal Panda Code task that you can open on your computer and read. So that already gives you the continuous part because you message it from your phone and then see the same work on your desktop. The trick is to make more than one bot. First, I make one called router and I give it DeepS v4.1 flash as its brain. Since this job is light and we want it cheap, in its instructions, I write that it only talks to me and hands out work and that chat replies stay under 100 words. Then I make a couple of worker bots with stronger models like one for building and one for reviewing. Bots can send work to each other with a tool called bot messagebot. The work goes to the other bot's own conversation and when it is done, the result comes back to the sender as an update. So the router stays clean. Each worker has its own context and you only hear from one agent. That is the two-layer design and you build it with a form. Now remember the experiment because a prompt isn't enough. So I also add deny rules on the routerbot for its shell and edit tools. Deny rules always win. So now it can't decide that the work is small and do it itself which is the same idea as deepseek removing the bash tool. And by the way, Panda Code has something called Panda Router and it is a different thing from the router in this article. Their router talks to people. Panda router picks a model. If you start a normal task and turn on an automatic team, it reads each assignment on your computer and picks the cheapest model that is likely to pass. And if a worker fails, the replacement moves to a stronger model. So for one big job at your desk, a team is the better option. For an always assistant, you want the bots. Now for the models, this is where Klein Pass comes in. Klein Pass is the $9.99 per month plan from the Klein team, and it gives you models like Kimmy K3.1 Pro, GLM 5.3, Quen 38 Max, and Deepsec V4.1 Flash. A setup like this runs a lot of sessions, so having one plan with a bunch of strong open models makes a lot of sense instead of paying for each provider separately. And you can check your 5-hour, weekly, and monthly limits on the client dashboard. To set it up, run npm install-g client, then run client off and sign in, and choose client pass. Panda code finds Klein after that, so you can pick it for a bot. I would put Kimmy K3.1 Pro on the builder since it is good at holding on to a long task and GLM 5.3 on the reviewer because different models make different mistakes and you need the Deepseek harness for the router. So run npm install-g at deepseek-ai/dsh and paste your API key in settings under providers. Let me show you how this looks. I connect the router to Telegram. The first time I message it, it gives me a pairing code and I approve that in the app so random people can't talk to it. That is basically the first filter from the article. Now I'll send the login page breaks on mobile. Can you take a look? The router gives me one short line and sends the work to the builder. While that runs, I send something completely different like what changed in the billing code this week. And that goes to its own conversation. So the two tasks don't get mixed together. In Panda Code, you can see each one as its own thread with every command and every file change. When the builder needs to do something risky, the approval comes to me in Telegram and I can just reply yes or no. Then when the fix is ready, the builder reports back and I get one short message from the router with the pull request link. If I change my mind, I just tell the router and it passes that on to the builder. And if anything looks wrong, slashs stop in the chat stops the bot and is scheduled. Next, the proactive part. Each bot has goals and an optional heartbeat which checks those goals on a readonly basis and reports back or proposes something. And it has schedules so you can make a small watchdog bot that runs every 30 minutes, checks your open pull requests and CI with the GitHub CLI and only messages you if something is stuck. It is a lot simpler than what DeepS describes, but it covers the same problem, which is that a process can look fine while the work is going nowhere. Then the persistent part. If your bots run on a laptop, they stop when it sleeps. So you can run panda code on a spare machine or a server with the pandic code serve command and your bots keep running there for a single long task. You can also pick a cloud provider in the run-on menu and the task keeps going while your laptop sleeps and the changes come back to a local work tree. Now where does client desktop fit? I would use it for the boring recurring jobs. It is an open- source app that runs outside your IDE with parallel sessions that each keep their own context. It has a schedule page where you pick the frequency, the prompt, the model, and the workspace. So, you can set up a nightly pull request review or a security scan on client pass and forget about it. You can also import old sessions from claude code or codecs and continue them on cheaper models. And there is a marketplace for skills and MCP servers. It is still you managing sessions, so it doesn't solve the attention problem by itself. But for fixed jobs that don't need a router, you don't need anything more than that. Now, let me be fair here. This is not what Deepseek describes. Pandaode bots only accept paired senders, so the bot won't sit in a public group chat and jump in on its own. And honestly, I think that is the safer default for now. A GitHub comment isn't a channel for a bot, so it can't follow your plan B from a pull request comment the way their agent does. Each chat thread is its own conversation with shared memory, not one global context. And the router in my setup depends on its instructions and rules, not on a proper system with subscriptions and pass through. If you want to try the real thing, you can look at the DSH super agent repo. It watches one GitHub repository and optionally fue and it has a panel that shows what needs a person. It is actually set up by an agent. So you can open a task in Pandaode and tell DeepSeek to read setup.mmd in that repo and set it up with you. But its workers run commands without approval as your user. So do this on a separate machine or a test repo. They also start any proactive work in a mode that only records what it would have done. And I would leave it like that until you trust it. So what do I think? I think DeepS is right about the main point. Models are not the only thing limiting us anymore. And adding more sessions to a screen doesn't fix that. The real idea here is simple. One agent talks to you, a bunch of isolated workers do the work, cheap code filters the noise, and something independent checks that the work is actually moving. You don't need their prototype to use that. You can set up a useful version with Pandaode bots this weekend. Run it on Klein Pass and DeepSeek for very little money and leave the fixed jobs to client desktop. It's not perfect, but it is a really good way to get past that limit of 3 to 5 sessions. All the links are in the description. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, [music] let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the super thanks option or becoming a member [music] by clicking the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye. >> [music]

items.title: I Built a Tiny Local Model That Outperforms Opus! (by using Orchestration)
items.summary:
PandaCode: https://github.com/aicodeking/pandacode
PandaOrchestrator: https://github.com/aicodeking/PandaOrchestrator

In this video, I'll show you PandaOrchestrator and Panda Router, a tiny local model I built to decide which model each worker in an agent team should use. I'll go through how it works, how I trained it on a budget with Ettin, Modal and an attempt-and-grade setup, and the numbers on 150 held-out tasks, including the escalation ladder that gets it close to perfect routing. Then I'll show all the new updates inside PandaCode: the router built into the app, the Team menu with Cheap, Balanced and Best teams, failover, model health, the model tier list, sub-workers, team messaging and the leaner architect. Finally, I'll run a Balanced team on a real task and give you my honest take on where it still falls short.

--
Key Takeaways:

🧠 Panda Router is a tiny decision model, not a chatbot: it profiles a task and plain code scores every model you can run on success, cost and spe
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: Hi. Welcome to another video. So, if you have been following the channel, you know that I have been building Panda code, which is my open source workspace where you can run Claude code, Codex, Kimmy, open code, and a bunch of other coding agents side by side. And one of the biggest parts of Panda code is agent teams where one lead agent, the architect, splits a task into assignments and hands them to worker agents that run in parallel. But, there was always one problem with this. The architect had to decide which model each worker should use, and honestly, it was not good at that. It would either put Opus on everything, which burns through your limits on stuff like renaming a variable, or it would pick something cheap for a task that clearly needed a stronger model, and then you would have to clean up after So, I built something to fix that. It's called Panda orchestrator, and inside it is a small model I call Panda router. Today, I want to show you how I built it, how it works, and all the new updates inside Panda code that make the orchestrator a lot better than before. So, let's get right into it. Now, the first thing to understand is that Panda router is not a chatbot, and it doesn't write any code. It's a tiny decision model. You give it a task and a list of models you can actually run, and it tells you which one should handle it. It reads the task and gives you a category, a difficulty from 1 to 10, the skills the task needs, and a few flags like whether it needs tools or images. Then, a normal piece of code, not a neural network, takes that profile and scores every model against it on chance of success, cost, and speed, and picks one. I kept the judgment in the model and the policy in code on purpose because you can test code. If the router makes a weird pick, I can see exactly why it made it, and I can fix the rule instead of retraining anything. Another thing I decided early is that the models are just data. Every model has a small JSON card with its skill levels, its price, its context window, and its latency. So, when a new model comes out, which is basically every other day now, you add a card, and that's it. You don't need to retrain the router to to about it. Now, let's talk about how I actually built it. Because this was a pretty fun one. The profiler is based on Eton, which is a family of small encoder models with an MIT license. They are trained on open data that includes code and every size shares one tokenizer. So, you can train a big one and distill it into a small one. So, I trained a 150 million parameter teacher on Modal and then distilled it into a 32 million parameter student. That student gets quantized to int 8 and exported to ONNX and the final file is about 31 MB. It routes a task in around 10 to 25 milliseconds on a normal CPU with no GPU and nothing about your task ever leaves your machine. The whole Modal training run cost me $1.67, which is kind of hilarious if you ask me. The data was the harder part. For the labels, I used DeepSeek-V4-1-Flash as a teacher and it labeled about 8,000 tasks for just $2.77. But, labels like this is difficulty six are only guesses. So, I also did something I call attempt and grade. I had real models actually attempt the tasks and then a strict judge graded every answer as a pass or a fail. That gives you real outcome data, meaning this model really did solve this kind of task and this other one really did not. I kept going with that until my OpenRouter credits literally ran out at around $44 and the DeepSeek balance ran out halfway through grading as well. So, yeah, this was done on a budget for sure. From those outcomes, I trained what I call a success head. It takes the task profile and gives you a calibrated chance of success for each model plus a lower bound. The router makes decisions on that lower bound, not on the optimistic number. So, it doesn't bet on a model that only looks good on paper. And the cost it compares is the expected cost, which includes what a failed attempt costs you. Because a cheap model that fails half the time is not actually cheap. There are also two small things in training that I really like. First, the difficulty loss is lopsided. If the router has to make a mistake, I want it to think a task is harder than it is, not easier. Because underrating a task is the expensive mistake. And second, I fine-tuned it on about 1,500 vague requests. Things like make the app better with no scope at all. Those get rated harder on purpose because a vague task really is harder for any model to get right. But the biggest idea in version four is the escalation ladder. Along with its pick, the router gives you an ordered list of models to try. You start on the first one. You check the result with tests or a type check or a review, and if it fails, you move one step up the ladder. And it never steps down, which means after a model fails, the next model is always at least as strong as the one that failed. Now, here are the numbers. And I tested these on 150 held-out tasks with real attempts with a nine-model pool. A single pick in the default mode solved about 77 out of 100 tasks for around $1 per 100 tasks. Always sending everything to GPT 6.1 solved solved about 79 for $1.11. So, a single pick from the router is already in the same range as always using the big model while being cheaper. But, once you let it escalate with at most two attempts, it goes up to about 91 out of 100. And the best case possible, where you magically know the right model for every task, is 94. So, with one retry, the router gets really close to perfect routing, which is just amazing to see. I also want to be honest about one thing. I trained a version five and a version six after that with more data and a fresh test set, and neither of them is the default. I wrote down the pass rules before running the evaluations, and both of them missed in at least one place. So, version 4.3 stays the default. Version six also caught a funny bug where answers longer than 6,000 characters were getting cut off before grading. So, they almost always failed, which made Sonnet look way worse than it really is. So, there's that. Now, I'm keeping the training part short here because there is a lot more to it than I can fit in this video. So, I made a separate members-only video where I go through all of it in detail. That covers where the 8,000 training tasks came from, how the teachers and judges were checked against each other, the model runs, the trick I used for vague tasks, the success head and how it's calibrated, and every mistake I made from version 1 to version 6 with all the numbers. If you're into that kind of stuff, you can join the channel through the join button, and it's right there in the members tab. Anyway, the repo is MIT licensed, and it comes with a CLI, an HTTP server, a Python API, and an MCP server, so you can use it with pretty much any agent, not just PandaCode. Anyway, now let's come to PandaCode, because this is where the router actually becomes useful for you. Panda router is now built straight into PandaCode. I ported the whole thing to Rust, and ONNX runtime ships inside the app, so you don't need Python. You don't need a server, and you don't need to install anything. The first time you turn on a team, PandaCode downloads the 35 MB byte profiler once from a pinned commit on GitHub and checks it with SHA-256. It never downloads at launch, and while it downloads, a simple keyword fallback picks models, so your team never waits on it. The router also sees every model of every coding tool you have installed. Before this, the automatic team only offered 24 models, six per tool, so things like Muse or the newer Kimmy releases could just be missing. Now it gets the whole list, and on my machine, it's picking from 45 rated models right now. Next is the team button in the prompt box. When you click it, you now get one simple menu with no team, cheap team, balanced, and best team. Cheap team picks the cheapest model whose chance of success clears a minimum that you set. Balanced weighs success against cost and speed, and best just goes for the strongest fit. New tasks start on whatever you used last, so you set it once and forget it. And this is where the escalation ladder comes in. In cheap and balanced teams, each worker starts on the cheapest model that's likely to pass. The architect checks the result, and if it fails, it replaces the worker, and the router picks a model stronger than every model that already failed on that assignment. After two retries, it stops and tells you that it failed instead of burning your limits in a loop, so you can actually see this in the thread. The dispatch note says something like routed to Haiku, ladder one of three, and if Haiku fails the review, the next note shows the step up and the models it skipped. Now, the next update is that teams are router first. Every assignment goes through Panda router by default. The architect only picks a model itself when you name one in your message, and it only falls back to its own model when the router has nothing left. So, if you say use Kimmy K3 for the front end, it will use Kimmy K3, and everything else gets routed. Then there's failover, which I think a lot of you will love. A lot of the time, a worker doesn't fail because the model is bad. It fails because the harness broke. Maybe you hit a rate limit, maybe the CLI crashed, maybe your login expired. So, now when that happens, Pandacode moves the worker to the same model on another harness you have installed like GPT-61S all through Codex instead of through Command Code, and runs it again on a fresh session. The architect sees a failover node with the real error, so nothing is hidden. And this connects to model health. When a model errors on a harness, Pandacode pauses it there for 10 minutes, and that doubles every time up to 2 hours. If two models on the same harness are paused, the whole harness is paused until something on it works again. Paused models never reach the router or the architect. The pauses survive a restart. And in settings, you can see each one with the reason, the time left, and an allow now button. Also, a crashed run no longer counts as a bad answer. Only a result that fails review moves the task to a stronger model, which is how it should have been from the start. You also get a switch for every harness and every model in settings under models for teams. So, if you don't want a certain model to ever be used by your team, you just switch it off, and the router, the fallbacks, and the failover all skip it. And harnesses with huge catalogs, like Open Code or Kilo, now only give your team their 10 most recently used models plus any you add with the add model button, so the router doesn't pick some random model you have never touched. Now, this next one is my favorite, and it's the tier list. In settings, you can drag your models into S, A, B, C, and D rows, just like a normal tier list, and your ranking actually steers the router. For a ranked model, the chance of success is 70% your tier and 30% the router's own rating at every difficulty. Your ranking also decides the order on the escalation ladder and the floor for never stepping down. One rank covers that model on every harness. And a model the router has no card for becomes pickable as soon as you rank it. So, if you think Kimmy K31 Pro is S-tier for your kind of work, you can just tell it that and the router will listen. It's a strong weight and not a hard override though. So, if you want your order to win completely, rank both models. Anyway, those are the routing updates, but the orchestrator itself also got a lot better in the latest releases. First, workers can now start their own sub-workers when a task really splits. It's one level deep with at most three running and six in total and only inside the worker's own files, so they can't step on anyone else's work. And while a worker waits on its sub-workers, it gets parked. Its process exits and frees about 250 to 390 epic types of memory. And it picks up again with their results without using an attempt or an architect round. Second, team messaging doesn't need polling anymore. Every team tool result now carries a short digest of unread messages. Agents can message the whole team or reply to a single message. And an urgent message reaches a running worker in the middle of its turn. There's also a shared notes board with up to 64 short facts, like an API shape or a decision the team made. And every new worker gets it when it starts. So, the front-end worker knows what the back-end worker decided without someone copy-pasting it around. Third, the architect rests while workers run before. It kept a spare process idling the whole time. Now, only an urgent message, a blocker, a failure, or finished results wake it up and everything uses fewer tokens, too. Workers get app instructions that are 80% shorter, about a third of the team tool text. And the architect's review turns are about a third of their old size. So, you get more work out of the same limits, which is quite great for sure. And you can actually follow all of this now. Every PandaCode tool reads as a sentence in the thread. So, a dispatch shows up as something like dispatch to workers with a card listing each worker's model, files, and status. Team messages show up as bubbles and the changes view now highlights which worker changed which lines, and it opens big diffs right away instead of freezing. So, let me show you how this looks when you put it all together. I'll pick balance team from the team button, and I'll give it a task like add dark mode to this app with a settings toggle, and make sure the tests pass. Now, watch this. The architect splits it into a few assignments and dispatches them all in one batch. You can see the small styling task got a cheap model, the settings logic got a mid-tier model, and the review got a stronger one. Each line tells you which rung of the ladder it is on. If we wait a bit, one of the workers comes back, and the architect runs the tests. Let's say one test fails. The architect replaces that worker with profile auto, and the router moves it to a stronger model, never a weaker one, and it's now done with every worker on the cheapest model that could actually do its job. Overall, I'm really happy with how this turned out. The whole router went from an empty repo to version four in about 3 days. It cost around $50 in total, and it's now running inside an open-source app that anyone can use for free. It's not perfect. The model cards are still estimates for a lot of the coding tool models. The success numbers look low because they come from a strict judge, so you should compare models with each other and not against 100%. And Intel Macs and x86 Linux still use the keyword fallback because there's no compatible Onyx runtime build for them yet. And escalation is only as good as the check the architect runs, so give it real tests if you can. But the upsides make it super worth it. You stop wasting your best models on easy stuff. You stop getting burned by weak models on hard stuff, and when a harness breaks, your team just keeps going. Both Panda Orchestrator and Panda Code are open source, and the links are in the description. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the Super Thanks option, or becoming a member by clicking [music] the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye. >> [music]

items.title: I Built Deepseek Stack that makes DS 4.1 Flash perform like Opus!
items.summary:
Join this channel to get access to perks:
https://www.youtube.com/channel/@aicodeking/join

DeepSeek Stack on GitHub: https://github.com/aicodeking/deepseek-stack
PandaCode: https://github.com/aicodeking/pandacode
Cline Desktop: https://cline.gg/desktop-aick
ClinePass: https://cline.gg/clinepass-aick

In this video, I'll be showing you DeepSeek Stack, my open-source pack of 29 ds- agent skills that fix the habits holding DeepSeek V4.1 Flash back, so it gets to around 80 percent of what Opus 5.5 does in my daily work while staying fast and super cheap. I'll start with the price difference and how to install it with one npx skills command, then set it up in PandaCode with DeepSeek's own harness, thinking on max, and show where Cline and the $9.99 per month ClinePass plan fit in. After that, I'll walk through every command: the core skills, the loops like plan-loop, verify-loop, unstick, review-loop, jury and best-of-n, the build and design skills, and the ship and understand skills. Fina
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: Hi. Welcome to another video. So, if you have been watching my channel for the last few months, you know that I have been using DeepSeek a lot. Like, a lot. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is now the model that does most of my daily coding work, and for the kind of stuff that I do every day, it honestly gets me to around 80%of what Opus 5.5 does. It is also really fast, and the price is not even in the same universe, but that 80%did not come for free. When I first started using it, it felt more like 60%. And when I looked at why, it was almost never because the model was not smart enough. It was because of habits. It would jump straight into code without a plan. It would say fixed without ever running the test. It would try the same broken idea four times in a row with small changes. And on long tasks, it would slowly forget what the goal even was. The good thing is that you can fix habits. You cannot make a model smarter with a text file, but you can make it plan, check its work, and stop when it is stuck. And that closes most of the gap. So, I went through a couple of the skill packs that have been getting really popular lately, took the ideas that actually help a cheaper model, threw away everything that was tied to one specific tool, and rewrote all of it to be shorter and clearer. Then I added my own loops that I have been using with DeepSeek, plus some much better design skills, because DeepSeek's default front ends are, let's say, not great. The result is called DeepSeek Stack. It is 29 skills. It is open source under the MIT license, and you can install it with one command. In this video, I'm going to show you how to set it up, and then walk you through every single command using Panda code with DeepSeek. And I will also show you where Klein and Klein pass fit into this, because they make a couple of these skills a lot better. So, let's get right into it. First, let's talk about the price, because that is the whole reason this matters. Opus 5 .5 costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at off-peak hours costs 15 cents per million input tokens and 60 cents per million output tokens, and cached input is about 3/10 of a cent per million. At peak hours, those prices double, but even then it is still more than 13 times cheaper than Opus on input and more than 16 times cheaper on output. And this changes how you should think about tokens. With Opus, you try to save every token. With Deepseek, you can spend extra tokens on quality and still pay almost nothing. Run three attempts instead of one. Get a second review and a fresh context. Run the tests again. A lot of the skills in this pack are built around exactly that idea. They spend a little more of a very cheap model to get a result that is much closer to an expensive one. Now, let's install it. Open your terminal in your project folder and run NPX skills at AI cooking {slash} Deepseek {slash} stack. It shows you the list of skills and asks which agents you use like Claude Code, Code X, Clyn, Open Code, and so on. If you want it in every project, add the {dash} G flag. And if you only want one skill, you can add {dash}{dash} skill and name like {dash}{dash} skill DS verify loop. Every skill starts with DS, so they do not clash with other skills that you already have. And they are just skill.md files, so they work in basically any agent that supports skills. Now, for the setup that I actually use, I run all of this in Panda Code. If you have not seen it, Panda Code is my desktop app for coding agents. It runs Claude Code, Code X, Kimmy, Open Code, Clyn, and a lot more in one window. And it supports Deepseek directly through Deepseek's own harness, which is called DSA. To set that up, run NPM install {dash} G at Deepseek {dash} AI {slash} DSH. Then in Panda Code, go to settings, then providers, and paste your Deepseek API key. Now, start a new task. Pick Deepseek in the model picker. Choose V4.1 flash and set the thinking effort to max. Please do not skip this part. Thinking at max matters more than any skill in this pack. When I tested this model with thinking off, the score dropped by almost 30 points. Now, Clyn and Clyn Pass. Clyn Pass is the $9.99 per month plan from the Clyn team, and it gives you a whole set of open models, including DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Kimmy K3.1 Pro, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, and Qwen 3.8 Max with really generous limits. Klein is also available inside PandaCode. So, you can run your main task on DeepSeek and send some of the work to Klein workers that use the other Klein pass models. That becomes really useful for the review skills, and I will show you that in a bit. Now, let's go through the commands. I have split them into five groups: core, loops, build, ship, and understand. Let's start with the core. The first one is/ds mode. This is the always-on working style, and if you only install one skill, make it this one. It tells the model to restate the task in one line before it acts, read the code before it edits it, make the smallest change, run a real command after every change, and never say done without showing the output in the same message. It also has a rule that I really like. If the same fix fails twice, the model has to stop and not try a third version of the same idea. And it keeps the context lean, so it reads only the parts of files that it needs and gives you a short final report. You can see the difference right away. I tell it to fix a bug in this project, and the first thing it does is write one line with the goal and the change that it expects. Then it reads the function and every place that calls it. Then it makes the change, runs the test, and pastes the result. That is it. No essay, no fake confidence. The second one is/ds principles. These are 21 engineering rules of thumb, each with a short trigger for when to use it. Things like fix the root cause and not the symptom, delete code before you add code, check validation at the edges of the system, and test what the user can see, not how the code works inside. You do not call this one often. The other skills point to it when they need it. The third one is/ds help. If you do not know which skill to use, type/ds help and describe the task, and it picks one for you and tells you why, which is great when you first install the pack, because 29 skills is a lot to remember. Now, let's come to the loops, and this is the part that made the biggest difference for me. /ds plan loop is for anything that touches more than one file. The model writes a numbered plan, and every step has a check that proves the step works. Then it reviews its own plan in a fresh pass, looking for missing steps, risky assumptions, and a simpler way to do it. It fixes the plan, and only then does it start coding, one step at a time, checking each one before it moves to the next. So, I give it a task to add a settings page with a dark mode toggle that is saved between sessions. It writes six steps to a plan file, and the review catches that it forgot to handle the first load before the saved value is read. That is exactly the kind of thing DeepSeek misses when it just starts typing. {slash} DS verify loop is the one I use the most. Edit the code, run the real check, read the real error, find the root cause, fix it, and run it again. It can do that at most five times, and then it has to stop and report. It also has to paste the final passing output, and it is not allowed to weaken or skip a test just to make it pass. This one alone stops most of the I fixed it lies. {slash} DS unstick is for when the model goes in circles. When the same error comes back after two fixes, it stops editing, writes down the assumption that all the failed fixes had in common, and tests that assumption directly. Most of the time, that is where the real problem is. If the assumption holds, it lists three different approaches, picks one, and starts again from a clean state. {slash} DS context reset is for long tasks. The model keeps a file called progress. MD MD with the goal, what is done with evidence, what comes next, and the key facts. It updates it after every step that it verifies, and when the context gets long, or the model starts to repeat itself or forget things, it moves to a fresh session that reads only that file. This works really well with DeepSeek because a fresh context with a good summary is usually better than a long context full of old tool output. {slash} DS ledger is close to that, but for long runs where you're not watching, it keeps a log with one row per decision, with what it did, why, and the evidence. It reads the log again before each step, so it does not drift away from the goal. And when you come back, you can read the log and trust what happened. /ds review loop sends the change to a reviewer with a fresh context. The author fixes what the reviewer finds, and they go back and forth until both agree for at most four rounds. The reviewer can be a fresh deep seek session or a stronger model if you have one. /ds jury is the bigger version of that. It gets reviews from two or three different models and loops until they agree. And this is where Klein and Klein pass come in really nicely. In Panda code, the deep seek session is the lead and it sends the review out as read-only Klein workers one on Kimmy K31 Pro and one on GLM 5.3, both through Klein pass. Different models make different mistakes, so they catch different things. And because it is all on a $10 plan plus cheap deep seek tokens, you can run this on every pull request without thinking about the cost. /ds best of n is my favorite way to spend cheap tokens. It runs three to five attempts at the same task in parallel, picks the strongest one as the base, and then takes the best parts of the others into it. With Opus running five attempts hurts. With deep seek, five attempts still cost less than one Opus run. In Panda code, each attempt runs as its own worker, so you can see them side by side. And/ds swarm is for wide jobs. It splits a job across parallel workers like auditing every route in an API or checking every page of an app, and then it merges everything into one report with evidence for each finding. Now, let's talk about the build skills. /ds sharpen is for when the task is vague. It restates what you actually want, makes the task deeper instead of bigger, and rewrites the prompt. It can also attack the plan to find weak spots before you spend any time on it. /ds blueprint makes the model design, the types, the function signatures, and the module layout first. You agree on the shape and then it fills in the code. For anything with a real data model, this saves a lot of rework. /ds tdd is for bugs. It writes a test that fails for the right reason first, and then makes the smallest change that makes it pass. /ds blast radius checks what a change could break outside its own diff, like other callers, config, saved data, or other services. And it proves the most important safety fact by running real code, not by writing a paragraph about it. Then we have the two design skills, and honestly, these are some of the best in the pack. I went through the most popular design skills on GitHub and took the strongest ideas from all of them. /ds design makes the model write a short design direction before any code with the purpose, the audience, the tone, and the one thing people should remember. Then it sets the fonts, colors, and spacing and checks the plan against one question. Would I make this same plan for any similar prompt? If the answer is yes, it changes it. It also has a list of banned defaults like purple to blue gradients, enter as the display font, emoji as icons, and the centered hero with three identical cards below it. Then it takes screenshots at desktop and mobile size and fixes what it sees. So, I ask it to make a landing page for a small coffee roaster. And instead of the usual gradient template, it comes back with a warm paper texture, a serif display font, and a layout built around the roast dates, which is just so much better than what Deep Sea gives you by default. /ds design audit is for a UI that already exists. It takes screenshots at both sizes, scores things like hierarchy, typography, color, spacing, states, accessibility, and copy with evidence for every score. Then it fixes the top three to five problems and takes new screenshots to compare. Now, let's come to the ship skills. These need the GitHub CLI. /dspr opens a short pull request that starts with the problem, not a long list of every file that changed. /ds watch PR watches the pull request through CI and the review bots. It fixes the real findings, pushes, and keeps watching until it is ready, merged, or blocked. It has a small Python script that checks the pull request in a loop so the model does not have to keep asking. /ds ship is the full thing. It takes a change all the way to a merged pull request with nobody watching. It proves the change, runs the review loop, opens the PR, watches it, and merges it only when all the checks are green and every finding is fixed or answered. It never uses admin bypasses and it stops and asks you before anything that it cannot undo. /ds ready does all of that, but stops when the pull request is ready so you can do the final merge yourself. This is the one I use most of the time. To be honest, DS adopt takes over someone else's pull request, branch, or agent thread, finishes the original goal, and keeps the credit for the people who started it. DS revive brings an old pull request up to date. And it first checks if the idea still makes sense with the current code. So sometimes the answer is just to close it. And DS PR comments make sure that any comment the agent posts for you is clearly marked as coming from an agent and does not leak anything that it should not. Now, the last group understand DS explain tells you how a piece of code works and why it is built that way in plain words. DS catch up gives you a short summary of what changed while you were away plus every decision that is waiting on you. This is great after a long panda code run with a bunch of workers. DS lessons finds the mistakes that agents keep making in your repo and turns each one into a type, a lint rule, or a test so it cannot happen again. And DS onslaught removes the AI tells from writing like filler phrases and fake enthusiasm from your docs, PR descriptions, and code comments. So that is all 29. Now, how do I actually use these day-to-day? It is pretty simple. DS mode is always on. For a normal task, I start with DS plan loop. The model works through it with DS verify loop and if it gets stuck, DS mode tells it to switch to DS unstuck. Before I merge, I run DS review loop or DS jury with the client workers on client pass if it is something important and then DS ready opens the PR and gets it green. For UI work, DS design replaces the plan loop and for big tasks, DS best of N or DS swarm because the tokens are so cheap. Now, let me be fair here. This does not make Deep Seek V4.1 flash into Opus 5.5. On the really hard stuff like deep debugging across a huge code base or problems that need a lot of creative thinking, Opus still wins and sometimes by a lot. The 80%is my feel from my own daily work, not a benchmark, so take it with a grain of salt. The skills also use more tokens per task because they make the model check its work, review, and sometimes run several attempts. But with DeepSeek, that extra cost is tiny, and I would rather pay for a model that runs the test than for a model that says it ran the test. And as always with DeepSeek, your code goes to DeepSeek servers. If you are working on something private for a company, check if that is okay first. Also, if you run big jobs, try to run them at off-peak hours because the price is half. So, what do I think? Uh I think this is the best way to use DeepSeek right now. The model was already smart enough. What it needed was a plan, a real check after every change, a rule to stop when it is stuck, and a fresh pair of eyes before it ships. That is what DeepSeek stack gives it. Put it in Panda code, had Klein and Klein pass for the extra reviewers, and you get something that feels really close to Opus for most of your work while being fast and costing pennies. The repo is linked below, and you can install it with NPX skills at AI Code King/DeepSeek-Stack. If you have ideas for more loops, open an issue or a pull request. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your [music] thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the Super Thanks option or becoming a member by clicking [music] the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye. [music]

items.title: Google's NEW EGM Skill Set + Deepseek is ACTUALLY INSANE!
items.summary:
Cline Desktop: https://cline.gg/desktop-aick
ClinePass: https://cline.gg/clinepass-aick
EGM on GitHub: https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model
PandaCode: https://github.com/aicodeking/pandacode

In this video, I'll be taking a look at the Elephant-Goldfish Model, or EGM, an open-source plugin from Google that makes your coding agent design a feature properly before it writes any code, and that installs into Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity. I'll explain the idea behind it, where a full-context Elephant agent writes the design doc and fresh, zero-context Goldfish subagents review it, and then show how to install it and run the brainstorm, draft, review and resolve commands. After that, I'll show you why it pairs so well with Cline and the $9.99 per month ClinePass plan, how to mix models for the Elephant and the Goldfish, and how to run it inside PandaCode. Finally, I'll talk about what it means that Google built this for the harnesses where developers already are.

--
Key T
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: Hi. Welcome to another video. So, Google has put out an open-source project called the Elephant Goldfish model or EGM for short. It's a plugin that helps your coding agent design a feature properly before it writes any code. And the part that made me stop and look twice is where it runs. It works in Antigravity, which is Google's own agent. But, it also has first-class install instructions for Claude Code, Codex, Claude Cowork, and even ChatGPT work. And because it's all just skills and sub-agent prompts, you can run it with Klein too, which is what I have been doing with Klein pass and the new open models on there. I'll show you that in a bit. Because I think that's honestly the best way to use this. That is kind of wild if you think about it. Google has Gemini, Gemini CLI, Jewels, and Antigravity. They are competing directly with Anthropic and OpenAI on coding agents. And yet, here is a Google repo where the second install command in the readme is Claude plugin install. They didn't do a half-hearted port either. There's a dedicated Claude code folder with its own sub-agent adapters and a separate Codex manifest as well. The readme says that thousands of Google engineers use this internally. If that's true, then it tells you something. Google engineers are clearly not using only Gemini tools and Google seems fine with saying that out loud. Also, the repo does say this is not an officially supported Google product. So, take it as a Google team project rather than a big company launch. Still, it's under the Google org on GitHub and it already has around 2,600 stars after about 6 weeks. So, there's that. Now, let's talk about what it actually does because the idea behind it is really simple and it makes a lot of sense. The whole thing is based on an essay by Dave Rensin called Elephants, Goldfish, and the new golden age of software engineering. The idea is that you use two kinds of agents. The elephant is the agent that remembers everything. It has your project context, your requirements, and every decision you made in the conversation, and it writes the design document. The goldfish is the opposite. It's a fresh sub-agent with zero memory of that conversation. It only gets the design document and the files that the document points to, and its job is to review it. And the reason this works is something that you have probably already noticed yourself. When you spend an hour talking to an agent about a feature, the agent and you both build up a lot of shared assumptions. Then the design doc gets written, and it reads perfectly fine to both of you because you both already know the missing parts. A fresh reader doesn't know them. So, when the goldfish reads it and says, "Wait, what happens when this webhook fails? Or what does this term even mean?" That's exactly the gap that would have bitten you during implementation. The third role is you. You make the tradeoffs, and you approve the design. The agents don't get to decide what gets built, which I think is the right call. Now, let's look at how to install it. In Claude code, you first add the marketplace by running Claude plugin marketplace add google/elephantgoldfishmodel. Then you run Claude plugin install egm@egm. For Codex, it's basically the same thing. Run Codex plugin marketplace add google/elephantgoldfishmodel, and then Codex plugin add egm@egm. And for Antigravity, you just run ag plugin install with the GitHub URL. One thing they mention is that you should install the whole plugin and not just copy the skills folder. The skills read the reviewer personas and the document standards at runtime. So, if you only copy the skills, it breaks. After that, start a new session, and you're good to go. Now, let's talk about the workflow. In Claude code, all the commands use the /egm: prefix. The first one is /egm:egm brainstorm. You give it a feature, something like add webhook delivery to this project. The agent asks you questions to clarify the idea, and then it sends out six goldfish reviewers in parallel, each looking at the idea through a different lens. One of them is a contrarian that basically asks why this feature needs to exist at all, and whether an existing library already solves 90% of it. Another one looks at cost, quota, and token economics. When that's done, you get a file called concepts brief.md with the direction you agreed on. Then you run /egm:egm draft. This turns the brief into a proper design document. And the nice part is that it doesn't dump the whole thing on you at once. It writes it section by section and stops after each section for your feedback and chat, which is how a design doc should be written anyway. After that, you run {slash} egm {colon} egm review with the path to the draft. This is where the goldfish really come in. The review has five stages. There's a zoom out review, which is a skeptical architect looking for things that are too complex or not needed. Then a comprehension review where a naive reader flags every term and acronym that isn't explained. Then a hostile design critic that looks at architecture, scaling, and risks. Then another zoom out pass, and finally, an implementation readiness check, which is a pragmatic tech lead making sure the plan doesn't leave any design decisions to whoever implements it. They do warn you that this gives you a lot of feedback by design, and they literally tell you to take what you think is relevant and ignore the rest. Then there's {slash} egm {colon} egm resolve, which helps you go through the findings and agree on what to change. Once you approve the design, you just tell your agent to build it. I also really like how strict the reviewers are told to be. The review skill bands flattery outright. The reviewers are not allowed to call your idea great or brilliant. They are told to lead with what is wrong or risky, and they are told to give the strongest counter argument to whatever you propose. If you have ever had an agent tell you that your clearly broken plan is an excellent approach, you will know why this matters. And there's a hard rule here that I think is the most important part. If your agent can't create fresh sub-agents, egm stops the review. It doesn't fake it in the same context because a review in the same context is not a goldfish review. That's a pretty principled decision, and it's also why the Claude code version has its own adapters. Each reviewer gets read-only tools and its own isolated context, so the goldfish actually stays a goldfish. There are a couple of extra skills as well. {slash} egm {colon} egm bootstrap goes through an existing code base from the bottom up and writes readme files for each folder, then summarizes them up to the root. So, the elephant has a map of your project to work with. And {slash} egm {colon} egm drift report compares your design docs with the current code and tells you where they don't match anymore. They recommend running that once a week, which is a good habit if your docs usually go stale the moment you merge. Now, it's not for everything and the repo is pretty honest about that. The readme itself says that for a small clear bug fix, you should just use your normal workflow. The FAQ also admits that design and review take time and that it may not pay off for small changes. It's meant for features where you actually need to make decisions first. And all these fresh sub agents will burn a lot more tokens than just telling the agent to build the thing. A single review can spin up five or six reviewers and each one reads your doc and the reference code from scratch. If you do that on a $20 Claude or Codex plan, you'll hit your limits pretty quickly. And that is exactly where Klein and Klein pass come in. So, if you don't know about it, Klein pass is the $9.99 warp per month plan from the Klein team. They went to the AI labs for volume discounts and you get a whole bunch of open models with 5-hour weekly and monthly limits that are really generous for the price. And the lineup just got a lot better. Kimmy K3.1 Pro is now the default model and they have also added MiniMax M3.1 flash and the new DeepSeek V4.1 flash alongside GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 flash and QN3 Mac Max. That's a really strong set of models for less than a single month of most premium plans. Now, the reason this pairs so well with EGM is that a goldfish review is basically a token hungry workflow by design. You want lots of fresh readers. You want them to read everything and you want to run the review again after you fix things. On a flat $10 plan, you just don't have to think twice about that. You can run the brainstorm, the draft and two or three review rounds on the same feature. And it doesn't feel like you're burning money every time a reviewer opens a file. The other thing is that you can mix models, which I think is really underrated here. The whole point of a goldfish is that it doesn't share the elephant's assumptions. Well, if the goldfish is a different model, too, it doesn't even share the same habits or blind spots. So, what I like to do is use Kimmy K3.1 Pro as the elephant because it's really good at long careful conversations and writing the design doc. Then I use GLM 5.3 for the hostile design critic and the implementation readiness check because it's very good at reading actual code. And for the lighter passes like the comprehension review, DeepSeek v41 flash or MiniMax M31 flash are fast and more than good enough. All of that is inside one $10 subscription, which is just amazing. Now, how do you actually run it in Klein? Klein isn't on Google's official list yet, so this is a bit more manual than the Claude code install, but Klein now supports skilled.md skills and sub-agents, and that's all EGM really needs. The skills are plain markdown, and the reviewers are just persona files in the agent's folder. In fact, for Codex, EGM doesn't ship any named sub-agents at all. It just has a general purpose sub-agent read the persona file first, and Klein can do exactly the same thing. So, clone the whole repo, not just the skills folder, point Klein at the skill you want, and let it spawn fresh sub-agents for the goldfish. Just make sure the reviewers really are fresh sub-agents. If they run in the same chat, you lose the whole point. To set up Klein pass in Klein, just install the Klein extension in VS Code or run npm install {dash} g Klein for the CLI, and pick Klein pass during onboarding. If you have already set it up in VS Code, the CLI picks it up automatically. And if you want to use Klein pass in some other agent, you can create an API key in your Klein account and use it with the Klein API base URL. Also, Klein is available inside Panda Code as well if anyone wants to use it there. And honestly, Panda Code fits this idea really nicely. In Panda Code, you have an architect that holds the whole task, and then it sends work out to separate workers that each start with only their own assignment. That's basically the elephant and goldfish setup already, so you can keep your main session as the elephant and send the goldfish reviews out as read-only Klein workers running Klein pass models all in parallel. Each reviewer really starts fresh, and you can see all of their results in one place. Now, coming back to the Google angle because I think this is the more interesting story. This feels like Google admitting that the agent harness doesn't really matter that much anymore. Claude code codex anti-gravity Klein they all support skills and sub-agents now. So, a workflow written once can run everywhere. The repo even says that no harness gets a fork of the skill text. It's one set of skills and personas and each harness just maps the word sub-agent to its own tool. So, if the real value is moving from the model to the process around the model, then it makes sense for Google to put that process wherever developers already are. And right now, a lot of developers are in Claude code. I think that's a smart move, to be honest, and it's also a pretty good sign for us because it means these workflows aren't locked to one vendor and they're not locked to one model, either. This came out of Google whose own agent runs on Gemini and here we are running it on Kimi GLM and DeepSeek through Klein. That's kind of the best part of all this, being open. Overall, it's pretty cool. The idea is simple, the implementation is thoughtful, it's free, and Apache 2.0 licensed, and it fixes a real problem that most of us hit with long agent sessions. If you are building anything non-trivial, I'd say give the brainstorm and review steps a try on your next feature and see if the goldfish catch something you missed. And if you want to do it without worrying about limits, run it in Klein with Klein pass, either on its own or inside Panda code. Using Kimi K341 Pro as the elephant and GLM 5.3 or DeepSeek V4.1 Flash as the goldfish is a really good combo for $10 a month. I'll leave the links for EGM and Klein pass in the description. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the super thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give [music] this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye. >> [music]
